background.definition: IM is a clinical syndrome characterized by fatigue, adenopathy, fever, and sore throat that is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

list.listitem: Active-duty military personnel and college students: 11 to 48/1000 persons/year
Aged 10 to 19 years: 6 to 8/1000 persons/year
Younger than 10 years or older than 19 years: ≤1 /1000 persons/year
Among persons 16 to 20 with sore throat, about 1 in 13 have IM.
Typical generalist in full-time practice will see an average of 1 to 4 cases per year.
Epstein-Barr virus

Infectious mononucleosis (IM) is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a herpes virus that replicates primarily in beta-lymphocytes but also may replicate in the epithelial cells of the pharynx and parotid duct.

Heterophile antibodies are produced during the acute infection. Viral capsid antigen (VCA)-IgG and VCA-IgM are produced earlier and are more specific for EBV infection than the heterophile antibody test ("Monospot").
Infection is primarily spread by saliva.

Obtain a white blood cell count with differential in patients between ages 10 and 30 years with sore throat, fever, and at least one of the following: significant anterior cervical adenopathy, fatigue, posterior cervical adenopathy, inguinal adenopathy, palatine petechiae, or splenomegaly. C
IM is very likely if either >10% to 20% atypical lymphs or >50% lymphs plus >10% atypical lymphs. C
Because false-negative results are very common early in the disease, patients with persistent symptoms should be retested. C
Use VCA-IgM if diagnosis is important (eg, pregnant woman, competitive athlete). C

list.listitem: Hoagland's criteria: ≥50% lymphocytes and ≥10% atypical lymphocytes in the presence of fever, adenopathy, and confirmed by positive serologic test.
These criteria are very specific, but not very sensitive (risk of false-negative results).

A diagnostic evaluation for IM should be ordered for febrile patients between the ages of 5 and 25 years with sore throat plus splenomegaly, palatine petechiae, or posterior, axillary, or inguinal adenopathy.
Splenomegaly and palatine petechiae, and axillary, inguinal, or posterior cervical adenopathy provide moderate evidence in favor of IM.
Absence of fatigue and absence of any cervical adenopathy provide moderate evidence against IM.

A systematic review of 17 studies reviewed the history and physical for diagnosing IM. The only clinical symptoms significantly associated with IM were headache (LR+ 1.19, LR– 0.72) and sore throat (LR+ 1.12, LR– 0.67). Useful physical findings included splenomegaly (LR+ 2.39, LR– 0.66), palatal petechiae (LR+ 1.32 - 11.4; LR– 0.57 - 0.94), and any lymphadenopathy (LR+ 1.26, LR– 0.37.
Most patients with IM have an absolute and relative lymphocytosis and an elevation in atypical lymphocytes.I

A systematic review of 17 studies evaluated hematologic parameters for the diagnosis of IM. Laboratory results of value included absolute lymphocyte counts greater than 4 x 109/L (LR+ 10.20; 95% CI 4.79 - 16.0) and the presence of atypical lymphocytes greater than 10% (LR+ 8.97; 3.39 - 19.5) or atypical lymphocytes greater than 40% (LR+ 50; 39 - 64). The combination of lymphocytes greater than 50% and atypical lymphocytes greater than 10% was also highly useful to rule in disease (LR+ 50; 8.4 - 162).

Heterophile antibody is of limited sensitivity during the first week of illness (up to 25% false-negative rate). Because false negative results are common, patients with persistent symptoms should be reevaluated in the second week.

Viral capsid antigen (VCA)-IgG and VCA-IgM are more accurate, but also more expensive and less convenient than heterophile antibody. It is helpful for patients in whom accurate diagnosis is particularly important, such as pregnant women and competitive athletes.
Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen (EBNA) is not detectable until 6 to 8 weeks into the infection; if positive in a patient with less than 4 weeks of symptoms it suggests previous infection.
Diagnosis of the viral agent is particularly important in pregnant women since CMV and toxoplasmosis are associated with pregnancy complications.
Two risk scores were developed and internally validated in a single University health center, with the goal of identifying patients presenting with sore throat who had at least a 10% risk of IM.

The IM-NoLab score assigned 1 point each for tonsillar exudate, absence of myalgias, and patient report of "swollen glands", and 2 points for lymphadenopathy other than anterior cervical (i.e. posterior cervicular). Patients with 2 or more points had a 27% risk of IM in the derivation cohort of 1341 patients, and a 22% likelihood in the validation cohort of 820 patients.

The IM-Lab score used hematologic parameters. Patients received 1.5 points for > 5% to 10% atypical lymphocytes and 3 points for > 10% atypicals. They also received 1 point for >= 40% lymphocytes, and 1.5 points for an absolute lymphocyte count >= 4.0. In the validation cohort, patients with 0 points had a 3.6% risk of IM; those with 1 to 2.5 points 12.5%; and those with 3 or more points an 88% likelihood of IM. The AUC was 0.933 in the validation cohort.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the evaluation of patients with suspected infectious mononucleosis.
For symptomatic relief consider NSAIDs or acetaminophen, throat lozenges or sprays, and gargling with 2% lidocaine. C
Corticosteroids should not be recommended routinely and should be limited to patients with impending respiratory failure due to airway obstruction. B
Antivirals and ranitidine have not been shown to improve outcomes. B
Corticosteroids are recommended if patients have significant pharyngeal edema causing respiratory compromise.C
Meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 339 patients found no benefit of acyclovir. A Cochrane review of 7 RCTs of antivirals found no clinically significant benefits for most comparisons.
Another study found no benefit of ranitidine.

Some small studies have found that corticosteroids may reduce fever and pain. However, a Cochrane review concludes that they are of poor quality that evidence is insufficient to recommend steroids for symptom control.Their primary value may be in patients with significant pharyngeal edema that threatens respiratory compromise. Another systematic review of steroids for any patients with sore throat found that there may be benefit in terms of pain relief.

Rash was thought to be very common with use of amoxicillin in patients with IM. However, the likelihood may not be as high as previously thought. An Israeli study found that only 29% of patients with IM treated with amoxicillin experienced a rash. A Chinese study of 767 children found little evidence that any antibiotic, including amoxicillin, caused a rash in children with IM.
Robuvit is an extract of French Oak wood. In a small manufacturer sponsored trial of 50 patients, those randomized to Robuvit vs placebo had a greater reduction in fatigue at 4 weeks.
Good supportive care with adequate hydration is most important.
Care should include rest, adequate hydration, and pain control using NSAIDs, acetaminophen, or 2% lidocaine gargle.
Hospitalization should be considered if tonsillar enlargement is causing or threatening respiratory compromise.
The most common complication is co-infection with group A beta hemoloytic streptococcal pharyngitis, which occurs in approximately 20% of patients.
The most important complications are splenic rupture (0.1%-0.2%) and peritonsillar abscess (0.2%).
Splenic rupture is most likely during the first 3 weeks of illness, is more likely in males, and is only associated with trauma in a minority of patients.
Ultrasound is not recommended for all patients, but may be helpful to confirm absence of splenomegaly when an athlete wishes to return to competition in less than 6 weeks.
Sore throat, fever, headache, rash, cough, and nausea usually last no more than 1 month. B
Most patients feel that they have recovered by 2 months. B
It is not uncommon for patients to have persistent fatigue (21% at 2 months) or persistent problems with sleeping too much (14% at 2 months). B
Sore throat, fever, headache, rash, cough, and nausea usually last no more than 1 month.
A study that followed 150 patients for 6 months found that fatigue resolved more slowly: 77% of patients were fatigued initially; 28% at 1 month; 21% at 2 months; and 13% at 6 months).
Sleeping too much persisted in 18% at 1 month, 14% at 2 months, and 9% at 6 months.
Sore joints persisted in 15% at 1 month, 6% at 2 months, and 9% at 6 months.
Most patients feel that they have recovered by 2 months.
Since there is no good treatment, prognosis and natural history are the same.
A history of IM is associated with an increased risk of multiple sclerosis.
Not routinely required.
Patients should remain well hydrated and take analgesics as directed for symptom relief.
Patients should notify their physician if they are feeling worse rather than better at any time.
Patients should not participate in contact sports that could cause splenic rupture for a minimum of 4 weeks.
IM is much less common in older patients.
Older patients with IM are less likely to have hepatomegaly and jaundice.

Order VCA-IgM to confirm or rule-out diagnosis.
